articles.title: Disney’s new Star Wars animatronics interact with guests using AI
articles.summary: The Anzellans from The Mandalorian and Grogu are being brought to life through three new animatronics that use AI to respond to guest interactions in real-time.
articles.body: As advanced and lifelike as the animatronic characters at Disney parks have become, they typically either stick to predefined movements and routines, or there’s an out of sight puppeteer helping make their behavior appear more spontaneous. That could soon change as Walt Disney Imagineering R&D has revealed three new Audio-Animatronic prototypes that rely on Amazon’s AWS cloud and AI capabilities to respond in unique ways to guest interactions in real-time. The three animatronics, named Vilo Vele, Kado Bre’a, and Jibu Bre’a, are based on the Star Wars alien characters called the Anzellans that were featured in The Mandalorian and Grogu film released earlier this year. The tiny bots will make their first public appearance in Las Vegas later this month where attendees of the AWS re:Invent conference will have a chance to interact with them, although the characters, and the technology powering them, could eventually find its way into Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge and other attractions at Disney’s parks. [Image: Disney’s new Star Wars animatronics don’t need a puppeteer to interact with guests in real-time. Unlike Disney’s Olaf robot that recently debuted, there’s no one secretly using a Steam Deck gaming handheld to bring the Anzellans to life. The animatronics instead each have hidden cameras and microphones they use to capture guest movements and verbal interactions which are processed by multiple AI models running on AWS cloud servers. One “fast-decision model” generates quick responses such as the animatronics quickly making eye contact so it appears as if they’re paying attention, while larger models plan out longer interactions. However, the Anzellans movements and verbal responses aren’t generated on the fly by AI. Every movement and line of dialogue that’s selected and triggered by the models is prewritten by Disney Imagineers to ensure the animations stay true to each character, including unique personality quirks for each one. Although AI helps guide their actions, the Anzellans never deviate from the script.

Speaking in his first interview since the layoffs took place, Sarandos explained that the reductions followed years of continuous expansion across the company’s large workforce. Unfortunately, it's a very rare occurrence. Obviously, my heart goes out to the folks who were impacted by it, but I think it has made the company healthier for the future,” he added.When asked specifically about the exits of top executives Bela Bajaria and Dan Lin, Sarandos commended their achievements while explaining how leadership needs shift as a business evolves.“Both did a fantastic job for us, and I'm very proud of what they've done. Every once in a while when you're in my seat, you have to look forward and say there's people who are good for the business at one stage who may or may not be good for it at the next stage, and you want to get ahead of that as far as you can,” Sarandos said.Netflix layoffs: What co-CEOs said after 1000 job cutsLast month, Netflix announced that it would lay off roughly 6% of its employees, or roughly 1,000 workers. articles.title: Some creators are skeptical of Instagram’s new affiliate program
articles.summary: A new integration connecting Amazon and Instagram accounts seemed like great news for influencers. But some are concerned about who’s benefiting from it.
articles.body: For years, influencers have come up with workarounds on social media to figure out how to share affiliate links with followers. A new integration between Instagram and Amazon was announced earlier this month as a way to make it easier for influencers to make money from affiliate links — but some content creators are suspicious about who really benefits. The new integration allows creators to connect their Instagram and Amazon accounts and automatically tag products with their affiliate links, from which they earn a commission when followers make purchases. Influencers will be able to embed up to 30 product links in a Reel or 20 in a feed post, but a permissions setting has led to concerns about what creators are actually agreeing to. In connecting an Amazon account, creators must agree to allow the retailer and its brand sellers to create ads from “any public content” that includes a related affiliate link. Influencers must also agree to acknowledge that brands can edit their content and use their “testimonial, caption or media” for ads. The wide-ranging permissions are giving creators pause. Some have urged peers not to connect their accounts without reviewing the permissions and understanding how the feature would affect earnings. People making money on social media spend years tweaking their content and strategy to maximize reach, engagement, and, by extension, their bottom line. For some, it appeared that they would be giving Amazon and its sellers the ability to use their content under unclear terms. On Instagram head Adam Mosseri’s post announcing the feature, influencers complained about the lack of clarity, questioned whether using the feature would decrease their reach (which some creators say happens when they link to outside products), and demanded answers to whether their commission rate would stay the same when Amazon or brands use their content for ads. Linking products through the new integration won’t reduce reach, Jimmy O’Keefe, Instagram’s director of product marketing, said in an email to The Verge. O’Keefe also noted that creators will continue to earn commission through affiliate links when Amazon boosts their posts, and that they can stop the boosting in settings or disconnect the integration entirely. There’s also a separate, manual way to add products without linking accounts, if a creator wants to opt out of having their content made into ads. Amazon has an enormous influencer program that reaches across social media platforms. It is so lucrative that some content creators are able to make a living almost exclusively by hawking products for sale on Amazon, building empires on the shopping habits of their followers. When it comes to putting those links in front of followers, though, social platforms have historically been a roadblock, hence the cottage industry of link-in-bio tools meant to circumvent limits. Slowly but surely, though, platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube — perhaps chasing the success of TikTok Shop — have added more and more shopping features. The result is that shopping and social media begin to feel more and more like the same thing.

articles.title: Colts vs. Texans live updates, inactives, where to watch: C.J. Stroud, Houston host Daniel Jones, Indianapolis in AFC South showdown
articles.summary: The Colts and Texans will open up Week 11 on "Thursday Night Football."
articles.body: The Indianapolis Colts and Houston Texans will open up Week 11 with an AFC South clash on "Thursday Night Football," with kickoff set for 8:15 p.m. ET at NRG Stadium in Houston. It’s a must-win game as both teams look to keep their playoff hopes alive amid a less-than-ideal start.The Colts (3-7) have continued to struggle this season despite a Week 3 win over the Texans to kick off their annual series. They managed to snap a five-game losing streak last week against the Miami Dolphins and will look to keep that momentum rolling against an AFC South rival.The Texans got some tough news on the defense this week, officially placing linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair on injured reserve with a groin injury that will reportedly require surgery. It’s the latest blow for the struggling unit, which blew a 17-0 lead to the Cleveland Browns in Week 10, officially falling to 3-6. They’ll also be without running back Woody Marks, who was ruled out after suffering a concussion last week, though David Montgomery will return from a groin injury for the contest.Follow along with Yahoo Sports for live updates, highlights and more as the Colts face the Texans in Week 10, airing on Amazon Prime Video.

articles.title: Texans run over ineffective Colts for easy 26-3 victory, winning first home game this season
articles.summary: Indianapolis essentially waved its white flag with eight minutes remaining, replacing Daniel Jones with Anthony Richardson.
articles.body: Houston Texans quarterback CJ. Stroud passed for 194 yards and three touchdowns, providing more than enough offense for a defense that shut down the Indianapolis Colts effectively in a 26-3 win on Thursday night.The Texans won at home for the first time this season after losing their previous five at Reliant Stadium. Stroud completed 21-of-27 passes with one interception. A second one appeared to be taken away in the second quarter before replay review ruled that Colts safety Cam Bynum didn't catch the ball cleanly.Nico Collins caught three passes for 58 yards and a touchdown, while Kayshon Boutte followed with two catches for 40 yards and a score. Rookie tight end Marlin Klein caught Stroud's third TD pass. The Texans' offense also benefited from the return of running back David Montgomery, back after a four-game absence due to a groin injury. The eight-year veteran rushed for 107 yards on 26 carries, keeping several drives moving on the ground. Emari Demercado also ran effectively, gaining 33 yards on five carries.However, the sharpest thing seen on the field Thursday night may have been the Texans' "Rivalries" alternate uniforms that harkened back to the Oilers' classic look. With the victory, Houston improved to 4-6 and stayed on the fringes of the playoff race in the AFC. The Texans play host to the Baltimore Ravens in Week 12. +2 for the Terminator 😤📺: @NFLonPrime pic.twitter.com/TzcavjrlrF— Houston Texans (@HoustonTexans) November 20, 2026 On the other side, the Colts could get nothing going with their rushing attack. Jonathan Taylor managed only 21 yards on 11 carries. That put more pressure on Daniel Jones to produce in the passing game, which did not happen.Jones completed 12-of-27 passes for 144 yards and an interception. He did connect on four passes of 20 yards or more, but that simply wasn't enough to move Indianapolis toward the end zone. He was also tackled for a safety by Will Anderson Jr. in the third quarter after the Colts were pinned at their 5-yard line on a 62-yard punt from Houston's Kai Kroeger. Anderson now has 11.5 sacks this season, tops in the NFL, after notching a career-high 12 last season.Anthony Richardson Drops Back, Feels Some Pressure, And Heaves It Up Deep.The Ball Sails Over His Receiver. And Goes Out Of Bounds.This Was One Of His First Shots Downfield In A Long Time.Gotta Shake Off The Rust Somehow.Next One. pic.twitter.com/XhDzFJNkqk— SM Highlights (@SMHighlights1) November 20, 2026 With just under eight minutes left in the game and the Colts trailing by 23 points, Colts coach Shane Steichen replaced Jones with Anthony Richardson. But he threw two incompletions on his first series, the only action he saw. Naturally, Steichen was asked if the Colts will make a quarterback change for their next game. "We'll evaluate everything," he said.Altogether, the Colts generated only 167 yards of total offense. Anthony Gould tallied 48 yards receiving on two receptions, followed by 30 yards and two catches from Ashton Dulin. Taylor had four catches, but only for six yards. Even kicker Spencer Shrader couldn't provide many points, missing two of his three field-goal attempts. One of those kicks was from 62 yards and was blocked.Indianapolis has lost six of its past seven games, dropping to 3-8 for the season. Yet four teams have worse records in a subpar AFC. Up next for the Colts is a home matchup with the New York Giants (5-3-1).

articles.title: YouTube is reportedly preparing to settle social media addiction claims for $3 billion
articles.summary: YouTube is preparing to pay $3 billion to thousands of school districts across the US to settle claims its platform harmed kids with an “addictive” design, according to Bloomberg.
articles.body: YouTube is preparing to pay $3 billion to thousands of school districts to settle claims that its “addictive design” harmed kids, according to Bloomberg. Sources tell the publication that YouTube reached the agreement “in principle,” and that the deal would also include new safeguards for teens. The settlement would allow Google to avoid a wave of lawsuits filed by US school districts that accuse YouTube, Meta, Snap, and TikTok of negatively impacting the mental health of teen users. The first “bellwether” trial of these federal multidistrict litigation (MDL) cases was supposed to start in Kentucky in June, but all four companies settled for a total of $27 million before it went to court. The next trial is set for February 2027 before an Oakland, California judge, with Meta, Snap, and TikTok as defendants. Google didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment. In August, Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion over 10 years to settle lawsuits filed by a group of 47 states, along with several districts and territories. It also agreed to implement stricter safeguards for teens, but is pushing TikTok and YouTube to do the same. As part of the agreement, Meta will only shell out the remaining $5.3 billion of its $17.1 billion settlement if YouTube and TikTok roll out similar changes and pay matching amounts. In March, both YouTube and Meta were found negligent in a separate legal battle over social media addiction.
